To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cancer cells release a signal that induces an ER stress response in recipient cancer cells that promotes their survival and resistance to chemotherapeutics.
prostate cancer cells that are undergoing an endoplasmic stress response release a signal that promotes a similar stress response in other cells.
tumor cells can transmit signals between themselves to enhance tumor growth and drug tolerance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the endoplasmatic reticulum ( ER ) stress response and its intercellular transmission in cancer.
the role of the endoplasmatic reticulum (the cell’s protein factory) in cancer development and treatment.
the role of the unfolded protein and endoplasmic (ER) response in prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the UPR is an adaptive mechanism of cancer cells that can be transmitted between cancer cells and that promotes cancer progression.
TERS is an adaptive mechanism by which tumor cells can survive in stressful environments.
the intercellular transfer of ER stress signals promotes tumor growth and resistance in cancer cells and that the UPR kinase IRE1 and its effector Wnt signaling are critical for these functions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ER stress response in cancer cells can be transmitted to other cancer cells and that this transmission promotes tumor fitness.
the ER stress response can be transmissible between cancer cells and can promote tumor growth.
cancer cells can use the unfolded protein response as a mechanism to enhance their survival and growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tumor cells can use the UPR to communicate with one another and to enhance the fitness and adaptability of the entire tumor.
tumor cells can communicate with each other through a UPR signaling mechanism that we term transmissible ER stress.

tumor cells can use TERS to improve their survival and fitness in response to stressful environments, and that TERS may be an important mechanism of intercellicular communication that promotes tumor growth and drug-resistance.
